quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Compare these two sentences: A) 'The students who studied hard passed the exam.' B) 'The students, who studied hard, passed the exam.' What is the key difference in meaning?
quests.targetClause: In A, only the students who studied hard passed; in B, all the students studied hard and all passed.
quests.completedSentence: Compare these two sentences: A) 'The students who studied hard passed the exam.' B) 'The students, who studied hard, passed the exam.' What is the key difference in meaning?
quests.ruleExplanation: In sentence A, the clause 'who studied hard' is defining - it narrows down which students we mean (only the ones who studied). In sentence B, the commas signal that 'who studied hard' is extra information - it applies to ALL the students being discussed, who all happened to study hard.
quests.nativeTip: Read each sentence and ask: how many students are we talking about, and does the clause narrow that number down?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "In A, only the students who studied hard passed; in B, all the students studied hard and all passed."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: My car, which I bought three years ago, finally broke down. Is the clause 'which I bought three years ago' essential to know which car is meant?
quests.targetClause: No - I only have one car, so the clause just adds extra detail.
quests.completedSentence: My car, which I bought three years ago, finally broke down. Is the clause 'which I bought three years ago' essential to know which car is meant?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'My car' already refers to one specific car - there's no need to narrow it down further. The clause 'which I bought three years ago' just adds extra, non-essential detail, which is exactly why it's set off with commas.
quests.nativeTip: Think about how many cars 'my car' implies - singular and already specific, or one of several needing narrowing down?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "No - I only have one car, so the clause just adds extra detail."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: The car that I left the keys in is now locked. Is the clause 'that I left the keys in' essential here?
quests.targetClause: Yes - without it, we wouldn't know which car is meant.
quests.completedSentence: The car that I left the keys in is now locked. Is the clause 'that I left the keys in' essential here?
quests.ruleExplanation: Without 'that I left the keys in,' we wouldn't know which car is being discussed - the clause is essential to identify it, which is why there's no comma and 'that' is a natural choice.
quests.nativeTip: Think about how many cars might exist in this context - does the clause help narrow down which specific one is meant?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "Yes - without it, we wouldn't know which car is meant."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence would still make complete, unambiguous sense if the relative clause were deleted entirely?
quests.targetClause: My manager, who has worked here for twenty years, approved the request.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence would still make complete, unambiguous sense if the relative clause were deleted entirely?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'My manager' already uniquely identifies a specific person - deleting 'who has worked here for twenty years' still leaves a complete, clear sentence: 'My manager approved the request.' The other clauses are essential for identifying which employee, book, or photo is meant.
quests.nativeTip: Try mentally deleting each clause - which sentence still identifies exactly who or what is meant, even without it?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "My manager, who has worked here for twenty years, approved the request."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Everest, which is the tallest mountain on Earth, attracts thousands of climbers each year. Can 'which is the tallest mountain on Earth' be removed without losing the sentence's core meaning?
quests.targetClause: Yes, because Everest is already a unique, specific name
quests.completedSentence: Everest, which is the tallest mountain on Earth, attracts thousands of climbers each year. Can 'which is the tallest mountain on Earth' be removed without losing the sentence's core meaning?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Everest' is a proper noun that already names one specific mountain - the clause just adds extra factual detail, so it can be removed: 'Everest attracts thousands of climbers each year' still makes complete sense.
quests.nativeTip: Ask whether there's any ambiguity about which mountain is being discussed, with or without the clause.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "Yes, because Everest is already a unique, specific name"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: The hikers who ignored the trail warnings had to be rescued. Can 'who ignored the trail warnings' be removed without losing the sentence's core meaning?
quests.targetClause: No, because it identifies which specific hikers needed rescue
quests.completedSentence: The hikers who ignored the trail warnings had to be rescued. Can 'who ignored the trail warnings' be removed without losing the sentence's core meaning?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The hikers' alone doesn't specify which hikers - the clause 'who ignored the trail warnings' is essential to identify exactly which ones needed rescue, so it cannot be removed without losing meaning.
quests.nativeTip: Ask whether 'the hikers' alone, without the clause, tells you exactly which group is meant.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "No, because it identifies which specific hikers needed rescue"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Comma Placement in Non-Defining Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence is correctly punctuated, given that the speaker has only one brother?
quests.targetClause: My brother, who works in finance, just got promoted.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence is correctly punctuated, given that the speaker has only one brother?
quests.ruleExplanation: Non-defining clauses need a comma both before AND after them. Since 'my brother' is already unique, 'who works in finance' is non-defining and needs both commas.
quests.nativeTip: Since there's only one brother, the clause is just extra detail - check that both commas needed for that kind of clause are present.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "My brother, who works in finance, just got promoted."

quests.completedSentence: Which sentence is correctly punctuated, given that the speaker has several brothers?
quests.ruleExplanation: Since the speaker has several brothers, 'who works in finance' is essential to identify which brother is meant - this makes it a defining clause, which takes no commas at all.
quests.nativeTip: Since there are several brothers, this clause is essential to identify which one - check that no commas are used.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "My brother who works in finance just got promoted."

quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The Eiffel Tower, which was completed in 1889, is visited by millions every year."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Comma Placement in Non-Defining Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
quests.targetClause: Paris, which is the capital of France, is known for its art and architecture.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
quests.ruleExplanation: Since 'Paris' is a unique proper noun, 'which is the capital of France' is non-defining extra information, requiring a comma both before and after it.
quests.nativeTip: Paris is a unique city name - check that the extra information about it is properly set off with commas on both sides.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "Paris, which is the capital of France, is known for its art and architecture."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: That Cannot Introduce Non-Defining Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence shown here is grammatically correct?
quests.targetClause: My grandmother, who taught me to cook, passed away last year.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence shown here is grammatically correct?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'That' can never introduce a non-defining clause - only 'who,' 'which,' or 'whose' can follow a comma. Since 'my grandmother' is unique, this clause needs commas, which rules out 'that' entirely.
quests.nativeTip: One specific relative pronoun is never allowed to follow a comma in English, no matter what it refers to.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "My grandmother, who taught me to cook, passed away last year."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: That Cannot Introduce Non-Defining Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Which version of this sentence is grammatically correct?
quests.targetClause: The Mona Lisa, which hangs in the Louvre, draws huge crowds.
quests.completedSentence: Which version of this sentence is grammatically correct?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'That' cannot introduce a non-defining clause, even when referring to a thing; 'which' is required here since 'the Mona Lisa' is a unique painting needing commas around this extra detail.
quests.nativeTip: Even for things, one particular relative pronoun is banned from ever following a comma.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The Mona Lisa, which hangs in the Louvre, draws huge crowds."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: That Cannot Introduce Non-Defining Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence is grammatically correct, given that the speaker owns several paintings?
quests.targetClause: The painting that hangs above my desk was a gift.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence is grammatically correct, given that the speaker owns several paintings?
quests.ruleExplanation: Because there are multiple paintings, this is a defining clause - no commas are needed, and 'that' works perfectly well here since defining clauses freely allow 'that.'
quests.nativeTip: Since there are several paintings, this clause is essential to identify the one being discussed - check for both the correct punctuation and pronoun choice.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The painting that hangs above my desk was a gift."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Who in Both Defining and Non-Defining Clauses
quests.grammarRule: Who in Both Defining and Non-Defining Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Which of these statements about the pronoun 'who' is true?
quests.targetClause: 'Who' can be used in both defining and non-defining clauses.
quests.completedSentence: Which of these statements about the pronoun 'who' is true?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Who' is flexible - unlike 'that,' it can introduce both defining clauses (no commas) and non-defining clauses (with commas), which is exactly why it replaced 'that' in the earlier grandmother and Mona Lisa examples.
quests.nativeTip: Think back to the sentences about 'my grandmother' and 'my brother' - did 'who' work in both the comma and no-comma versions?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "'Who' can be used in both defining and non-defining clauses."

quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The nurse who checked my vitals was very kind."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Who in Both Defining and Non-Defining Clauses

quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "My doctor, who has treated me for years, finally retired."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Why do sentences about specific, named people or places (like 'Albert Einstein' or 'Tokyo') almost always use non-defining clauses?
quests.targetClause: Because a proper noun already uniquely identifies one specific person or place, so any extra clause is additional, not essential, information.
quests.completedSentence: Why do sentences about specific, named people or places (like 'Albert Einstein' or 'Tokyo') almost always use non-defining clauses?
quests.ruleExplanation: A proper noun like 'Albert Einstein' or 'Tokyo' already picks out one specific, unique thing - there's nothing left to narrow down, so any relative clause attached to it is automatically extra, non-defining information.
quests.nativeTip: Think about what a proper noun like a name or a capital city already tells you, before any clause is even added.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "Because a proper noun already uniquely identifies one specific person or place, so any extra clause is additional, not essential, information."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Comma Placement in Non-Defining Clauses

quests.completedSentence: Which sentence about a named individual is correctly punctuated?

quests.nativeTip: A named individual is already uniquely identified - check that the extra biographical detail is set off with commas on both sides.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "Albert Einstein, who developed the theory of relativity, never learned to drive."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Compare: A) 'My brother who lives in Paris is a doctor.' B) 'My brother, who lives in Paris, is a doctor.' What does sentence A imply that sentence B does not?
quests.targetClause: That the speaker has more than one brother.
quests.completedSentence: Compare: A) 'My brother who lives in Paris is a doctor.' B) 'My brother, who lives in Paris, is a doctor.' What does sentence A imply that sentence B does not?
quests.ruleExplanation: Sentence A implies the speaker has more than one brother, and 'who lives in Paris' distinguishes this one from the others. Sentence B, with commas, implies the speaker has only one brother, and the Paris detail is just additional information.
quests.nativeTip: Ask why sentence A would need to specify 'who lives in Paris' at all - what would that clause be narrowing down?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "That the speaker has more than one brother."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Compare: A) 'The employees who finished the training received certificates.' B) 'The employees, who finished the training, received certificates.' Which sentence implies that ALL the employees finished the training?
quests.targetClause: Sentence B
quests.completedSentence: Compare: A) 'The employees who finished the training received certificates.' B) 'The employees, who finished the training, received certificates.' Which sentence implies that ALL the employees finished the training?
quests.ruleExplanation: Sentence B, with commas, implies that all the employees (already a defined group) finished the training - it's just extra information. Sentence A implies only some employees finished, and the clause identifies which ones.
quests.nativeTip: Ask whether the clause is narrowing down a specific group, or simply adding a fact true of everyone already being discussed.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "Sentence B"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Comma Placement in Non-Defining Clauses
quests.questionSentence: A company has one CFO and wants to announce, without any ambiguity, that this one CFO is resigning, mentioning her 15 years of service as extra background. Which sentence should they use?
quests.targetClause: Our CFO, who has been with the company for 15 years, is resigning.
quests.completedSentence: A company has one CFO and wants to announce, without any ambiguity, that this one CFO is resigning, mentioning her 15 years of service as extra background. Which sentence should they use?
quests.ruleExplanation: Commas correctly signal that 'who has been with the company for 15 years' is extra background information about the one and only CFO, avoiding any false implication that there are multiple CFOs.
quests.nativeTip: Since there's only one CFO, the tenure detail is extra background, not identifying information - check the punctuation matches that.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "Our CFO, who has been with the company for 15 years, is resigning."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Compare: A) 'The books that are overdue must be returned by Friday.' B) 'The books, which are overdue, must be returned by Friday.' Which sentence implies that only SOME of the books are overdue?
quests.targetClause: Sentence A
quests.completedSentence: Compare: A) 'The books that are overdue must be returned by Friday.' B) 'The books, which are overdue, must be returned by Friday.' Which sentence implies that only SOME of the books are overdue?
quests.ruleExplanation: Sentence A, with no commas, implies that only some books (the overdue ones) must be returned - the clause narrows down which ones. Sentence B implies all the books being discussed are overdue.
quests.nativeTip: Ask whether the clause is narrowing down a subset of books, or describing a fact true of all the books already mentioned.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "Sentence A"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: A hospital memo reads: 'Patients who show symptoms of the virus must be isolated immediately.' What does this imply about which patients must be isolated?
quests.targetClause: Only the patients showing symptoms - not all patients.
quests.completedSentence: A hospital memo reads: 'Patients who show symptoms of the virus must be isolated immediately.' What does this imply about which patients must be isolated?
quests.ruleExplanation: Since there are no commas, 'who show symptoms of the virus' is a defining clause - it narrows down which patients specifically must be isolated, not all of them.
quests.nativeTip: Since there's no comma, this clause is essential - what job does an essential clause do?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "Only the patients showing symptoms - not all patients."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: If the memo instead read: 'Patients, who show symptoms of the virus, must be isolated immediately,' what would this incorrectly imply?
quests.targetClause: That every patient in the hospital shows symptoms and must be isolated.
quests.completedSentence: If the memo instead read: 'Patients, who show symptoms of the virus, must be isolated immediately,' what would this incorrectly imply?
quests.ruleExplanation: With commas, 'who show symptoms' becomes non-defining - it would incorrectly suggest that ALL patients show symptoms and must be isolated, which is a serious and dangerous change of meaning in a hospital setting.
quests.nativeTip: With commas, the clause becomes extra information about a group already fully defined - so who does 'patients' refer to now?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "That every patient in the hospital shows symptoms and must be isolated."
